findings.title: Second downsize definition overrides the existing width/height API
findings.body: Ruby does not support method overloading by arity. This new three-argument downsize definition replaces the width/height version defined immediately above it at lines 145-147. Existing callers using downsize(from, to, width, height) will now treat width as a complete dimensions string and height as opts, producing wrong geometry or a TypeError, while callers passing width, height, and opts will raise ArgumentError. The old signature must be retained compatibly or every existing caller updated.

findings.title: In-place downsizing ignores conversion failure and can destroy the upload
findings.body: OptimizedImage.downsize returns false when conversion or optimization fails, but this call ignores the result and uses the same tempfile path as both input and output. A failed or partial ImageMagick/ImageOptim operation can therefore truncate or corrupt the only copy of the uploaded file, after which the loop retries the failed operation up to five times and line 72 proceeds with whatever remains. Downsizing should write to a separate file, check the result, and only replace the original after success.

findings.title: No server-side size limit is enforced before expensive image conversion
findings.body: The 10 MB limits added elsewhere are only in client-side JavaScript and in the URL-download branch. A direct multipart request can bypass JavaScript and submit a much larger image, causing this code to run as many as five full ImageMagick and ImageOptim passes before Upload.create_for performs its normal size validation. An authenticated user can consequently trigger very large CPU, memory, and disk consumption, including with a highly compressed image that expands greatly when decoded. The controller should enforce the intended maximum input size server-side before invoking downsizing.

findings.title: Downsizing is applied unsafely to SVG and animated image originals
findings.body: The condition accepts every filename considered an image and sends it through convert with the first-frame selector. This bypasses the SVG special case elsewhere in OptimizedImage, where SVG files are copied rather than converted, so an oversized vector can be rasterized, invalidated, or changed in format. Likewise, when animated thumbnails are disabled, an animated GIF original is reduced to its first frame rather than merely having a static thumbnail. SVG handling and preservation of animation for the stored original need separate treatment.

findings.title: Hard-coded 10 MB client limit ignores per-type site settings
findings.body: validateUploadedFile receives a type and previously used the corresponding max_image_size_kb or max_attachment_size_kb setting. Replacing that lookup with a fixed 10 MB value means attachments larger than 10 MB are rejected even when the site allows them, while non-image attachments above a lower configured attachment limit pass the client check, are not downsized by the server, and then fail only after being uploaded. The same hard-coded value is repeated for the 413 error at line 246. The image pre-downsizing allowance should not replace attachment validation or disregard configured limits.

findings.title: No tests cover the new downsizing behavior
findings.body: The pull request adds a percentage-based OptimizedImage.downsize form, a five-attempt controller loop, changed client limits, and changed download limits, but includes no spec or JavaScript test changes. There is therefore no coverage proving percentage geometry works, that the loop terminates at the configured byte limit, that conversion failure preserves or rejects the upload safely, or that animated and vector images retain their expected format.
